summary:
Lunar Horizon is a mission-grade lunar astrodynamics platform that integrates 10 years of NASA JPL DE440 ephemerides (2026-2036 across 122 streaming binary chunks) with high-resolution LRO LOLA topographic ray-tracing.
Engineered for NASA's lunar exploration challenges, the application models continuous solar power availability and direct Earth-to-Moon (DTE) radio line-of-sight across all 16 Artemis South Pole candidate landing sites and custom coordinates. Key capabilities include 360-degree panoramic crater-rim skyline silhouettes, an interactive 3D lunar globe, an isotropic 1:1 celestial scaling inset, a multi-scenario comparison matrix, and a "Plan B" launch-slip screening tool.
Accurate surface illumination is paramount at the lunar South Pole, where grazing solar elevation angles within +/- 1.5 degrees cast extreme dynamic shadows that threaten lander power reserves and communication links. Lunar Horizon delivers real-time, peer-reviewed astrodynamic analysis to identify safe landing windows, prevent fatal freezes in permanent shadow regions, and maximize mission success for crewed and robotic surface operations.
details:
Lunar Horizon

A browser-based platform for modeling sunlight, terrain shadows, and Earth visibility at the Moon’s South Pole, with no server and no installation.

Overview

Lunar Horizon helps mission planners answer a hard question: when is a lunar landing site lit, and when can it see Earth?

Near the lunar poles, the Sun never climbs more than about 1.54° above or below the horizon. Even modest terrain features cast shadows tens of kilometers long, and a site that looks well lit on average can sit in darkness for days. Lunar Horizon models this extreme lighting geometry for all 16 NASA Artemis candidate landing sites, plus any custom coordinates, across a 10-year window from 2026 to 2036.

How It Works

The platform runs entirely in the browser on a two-tier physical modeling engine.

Tier 1: High-precision ephemeris propagation

  • Positions come from NASA JPL DE440/DE441 planetary and lunar ephemerides instead of static approximations.
  • Data is streamed in 122 binary chunks and evaluated with Chebyshev polynomial expansions.
  • IAU/NAIF SPICE frame rotations (MOON_ME_DE421 and moon_080317.tf) place the Sun and Earth in the lunar surface frame.

Tier 2: Topographic ray-tracing

  • Terrain comes from LOLA digital elevation models aboard NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), combined with the horizon modeling approach of Barker et al. (2021).
  • For each site, a 360° terrain silhouette is built, and the Sun and Earth are tested against it at every time step.
  • The calculation accounts for the Sun’s 0.53° disk grazing the horizon, lunar libration (up to ±8.1° in longitude and ±6.7° in latitude), and mast heights from 0 m to 12 m.

Key Features

  • 360° Panoramic Skyline and Radar: live Sun and Earth azimuth, elevation, and terrain clearance
  • Timeline Dock and Playback Engine: hour-by-hour simulation with automatic shadow-transition logging
  • Multi-Scenario Comparison Matrix: side-by-side trade studies of power curves, slopes, and cold-soak duration
  • Multi-Year Insolation Heatmap: seasonal availability that reflects the 29.53-day synodic cycle and the 18.61-year nodal precession
  • Launch-Slip Engine (“My Landing Slipped. What Now?”): recalculates lighting for delayed landings, flags battery freeze risk, and recommends alternative sites
  • Benchmark Validation Suite: checks against NASA JPL testpo.440 reference vectors (error below 2.1×10⁻¹⁷ AU), with 12 precision gates and 182 benchmark vectors
  • Exploration Primer and Glossary: an educational reference on polar lighting, cold traps, and libration

Benefits

  • Zero-install access. Everything runs client-side, so no software setup or server compute is required, and results update near-instantly.
  • Contingency planning. Launch delays of days or weeks can be evaluated immediately, including whether a lander arrives in daylight or darkness.
  • Trade-study support. Candidate sites can be compared on maximum night duration, terrain slope, and Earth communication gaps against operational thresholds.
  • Honest visuals. Views are rendered at true 1:1 scale, avoiding the vertical exaggeration that misleads polar shadow analysis.
  • Verifiable results. Outputs trace back to authoritative NASA data and a built-in validation suite.

What Makes It Creative

  • True-scale celestial view. Many visualization tools exaggerate crater heights by 3× to 5×. Lunar Horizon uses a 1:1 angular viewport (2° to 16° field of view), so the Sun (0.53°) and Earth (1.91°) appear at their real sizes rising and setting behind real topography.
  • Dual-cycle season mapping. The multi-year heatmap shows how the monthly synodic cycle interacts with the 18.61-year nodal precession, revealing how polar seasons evolve over a decade.
  • Launch slip as a variable. Instead of assuming a fixed timeline, the platform treats delay as an input and responds with alternatives.

Factors Considered

  • Grazing sunlight: with solar elevation limited to about ±1.54°, sub-degree terrain accuracy is essential.
  • Libration: the Moon’s apparent wobble is included in every Earth azimuth and elevation calculation to keep direct-to-Earth communication predictions accurate.
  • Cold soaks: solar-powered landers without nuclear heaters risk battery freezing when unpowered nights exceed roughly 100 to 120 hours, so constraint gates automatically flag unviable sites.
  • Mast height: raising an antenna or solar array lowers the apparent horizon (Δθ ≈ √(2h/R_M)), and the effect is computed in real time.
  • Data provenance: every result is tied to named kernels, datasets, and published methods.

Intended Impact

Lunar Horizon is intended to support mission architects, flight planners, researchers, and students evaluating landing sites for NASA Artemis crewed missions and Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) robotic missions. As a transparent, open-access alternative to costly closed-source tools such as STK and FreeFlyer, the platform lowers the barrier to serious astrodynamics work and turns raw data from the Planetary Data System and NAIF SPICE into clear, actionable dashboards.

Tools and Technologies

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES2023+), GLSL, HTML5 Canvas, SVG, CSS3, Python 3.11
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, Three.js/WebGL, Tailwind CSS, KaTeX, Lucide Icons, Lenis
  • Data and ephemerides: NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (de440s.bsp, naif0012.tls, pck00011.tpc, moon_pa_de421_1900-2050.bpc), LRO LOLA gridded data from the PDS Geosciences Node, ASU LROC Featured Candidate Landing Sites Atlas
  • Development and hosting: Git, GitHub, Cloudflare Pages
